passage:
Sunday, late. Sent the money home again and felt two things at once: proud, and a tightness in my chest. Proud because Usha's college fees are covered and Appa's knee check-up won't be put off. Tight because my Pune rent eats most of what is left, and last month I skipped a trip with friends and told nobody why. That is how resentment starts, I think.

So tonight I finally said it on the call. "I can send a fixed amount every month, but I need to keep some savings too." Amma went quiet, then said, "Why didn't you tell us before? We never wanted you to have nothing." Appa took the phone and agreed we will look at the plan again every six months. Usha sent me a heart sticker.

Maybe tonight I will sleep better.
Anand

qa.q: Whose college fees does Anand say are covered?
qa.a: Usha's college fees are covered.

qa.q: What is Anand feeling when the money goes home?
qa.a: Anand feels proud and also tight-chested with the weight of duty, worrying that quiet resentment could start.

qa.q: What choice did Anand make on the call, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Anand told Amma plainly that a fixed amount was possible along with some savings, and Appa agreed to review the plan every six months.

qa.q: How does Amma see Anand's situation once it is spoken aloud?
qa.a: Amma is surprised and a little worried, saying the family never wanted Anand to have nothing, so Amma would rather know than have the sacrifice hidden.

grounding: A young worker sends part of a salary home, feels pride and duty together, and talks openly about what is sustainable.

passage:
Farhan, twenty-four, came home to his village near Moradabad on Eid leave from his factory job in Surat. His mother had repainted the house with the money he'd sent. His father introduced him to neighbours: "My son, he runs this house now."
Farhan smiled, proud, and something heavy settled on his chest.
That night, his younger brother Vishal whispered, "Bhaijaan, Abbu wants a motorbike next. He's told everyone." Farhan stared at the ceiling. He'd skipped the doctor for his back pain to send extra last month.
In the morning he sat with his father on the charpai. "Abbu, I'm glad I can help. But after rent and food in Surat, I can send only what I send now. No more. A motorbike isn't possible this year."
His father looked away, then nodded slowly. "Why didn't you say before?"
"I was scared you'd think less of me."
"Never," his father said, and put a hand on his shoulder.

qa.q: What did Farhan's mother do with the money he sent?
qa.a: She had repainted the house with the money he'd sent.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when something heavy settled on his chest?
qa.a: Farhan felt proud and burdened at once, pleased to support his family but weighed down by growing expectations.

qa.q: Why was talking to Abbu openly a wise choice?
qa.a: Telling Abbu honestly what he could manage prevented more strain and quiet resentment, and let his father understand instead of expecting more.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel about his brother's situation?
qa.a: Vishal seems worried for Farhan, which is why he quietly warns him about the motorbike.

grounding: A young worker who sends money home feels pride and heavy duty, and talking openly with his father about what is sustainable prevents resentment.

passage:
In the shared dormitory in Singapore, Jin, twenty-five, sat on his bunk after a twelve-hour shift and transferred money home to his parents in Malaysia, as he did every month. His mother's message came back: a photo of his little sister's new school uniform, and a heart.
He smiled. Then he opened his own account and saw how little was left.
His bunkmate Javier, from the Philippines, noticed. "You look like me last year."
"I'm proud to help," Jin said. "But I've had the same shoes for two years."
"I told my family exactly what I can send," Javier said. "Not as much as they wanted. My mother cried, then she said she didn't want me hurting. Things are better now."
Jin thought about it all week. On Sunday, he called his mother and said, gently, "Ma, I want to keep helping. But I need to talk about what I can manage."

qa.q: What did Jin's mother send a photo of?
qa.a: She sent a photo of his little sister's new school uniform, and a heart.

qa.q: What was Jin feeling when he saw how little was left?
qa.a: Jin felt proud of helping, but also strained and worried about his own needs.

qa.q: What helped Jin decide to speak up?
qa.a: Javier's story showed that telling family honestly what you can manage can lead to understanding, not rejection.

qa.q: How might Jin's mother feel when he raises the topic?
qa.a: She might feel surprised and a little sad, but, like Javier's mother, likely wants him not to be hurting.

grounding: Outside India, a young worker sends money home with pride and duty, and a friend's example encourages an open talk about what is sustainable.

passage: On salary day, Sabina sat in the office pantry with her phone, sending the usual transfer home to Siliguri. Her brother's school fees, Abba's medicines, the roof. She felt the small warm pride she always felt, and then, a minute later, a tightness in her chest. Her own rent was due on Friday. Hansa, from accounts, set down two cups of tea. "You look like someone who has just paid everyone except herself." Sabina laughed, then didn't. "If I send less, Ammi will think I've changed. If I don't, I can't breathe here." "Have you ever told her the numbers? Your side, I mean." "No. It feels rude." "It might feel like trust to her." That evening Sabina called home and, for the first time, said out loud what the city cost her.

qa.q: Where did Sabina send the transfer?
qa.a: She sent it home to Siliguri.

qa.q: What did Sabina feel after sending the money?
qa.a: Sabina felt proud and warm at first, then a tight worry in her chest because her own rent was due.

qa.q: What did Hansa suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Hansa suggested sharing Sabina's side of the numbers with Ammi, since open talk about what can be kept up prevents quiet resentment.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel when Sabina explains what the city costs?
qa.a: Ammi may be surprised at first, but could also feel trusted and relieved to understand, rather than thinking Sabina has changed.

grounding: It illustrates a young worker who sends part of a salary home with both pride and heavy duty, and begins to talk openly with family about what is sustainable.
